Scoring Streamlining: Point counting has been reduced by replacing some immediate point rewards with card draws, which speeds up the early game
Pattern Completion: Players can now perform "partial completes" (2 out of 3 requirements) to discard a difficult pattern and get a new one, though they forfeit the full bonus
Journaling: Completed patterns are "journaled" (tucked under the player board) and provide points at specific "live event gates" on the score track
Drafting: The game uses a "pick and pass" drafting phase for DNA cards before entering the scoring phase
Row Completion: Completing specific rows on the board provides tokens in descending order of value

Player Board Clarity: One player found the player board confusing due to a lack of biology background and noted that the "not purple" requirement for speckled kernels is too small to read easily in TTS

Victory Paths: A concern was raised that focusing on score track rewards (DNA cards) may be less viable than simply drawing cards through patterns, potentially creating a single dominant path to victory
Reward Scaling: Suggestion to increase the value of rewards on the score track to make that strategy more competitive

Row Bonus Balance: A suggestion was made to use a sliding scale (e.g., 5, 4, 3, 2) for row completion bonuses so that players who strategically complete rows first are rewarded more than those who simply fill the last remaining spot
Publication: The team decided to sign the game for publication
Core Structure: The team confirmed that the core gameplay loop and theme are successful and do not require fundamental changes
Contracting: The team will send a contract to the designers

TAM: Okay, biggest changes: the row completion tokens are now in descending order — complete a row in that section, you get the top token. That was John's suggestion. The other change is pattern cards — you can now do a partial complete. If you complete two of the three, you don't get the full bonus, but you get to journal it — tuck it under your player board. That matters because there are now score track gates where you get one point for each journaled pattern. It's also useful if you have a difficult pattern you just want to get rid of.

When you complete a pattern, you journal it and you might get a card bonus. You get the new pattern card at the end of your turn, not immediately — so you can only complete one pattern per turn, and people aren't waiting around while you deliberate.
Kristina: There's another major change — on the board, when you place a kernel you used to get two points, now you get a card. It speeds up the game and reduces fiddly point counting.

Audio Script
The Story
In 1947, Barbara McClintock discovered something that would change biology forever.
Working alone in a cornfield at Cold Spring Harbor, New York, she found that genes don’t just sit still. They jump.
The scientific establishment ignored her for thirty years. She won the Nobel Prize at eighty-one.
McClintock’s Maize is a strategy card game that puts that discovery on the table.
The Market
McClintock’s Maize sits at the intersection of three growing markets — strategy gaming, science education, and games celebrating women in history.
It plays in 45 minutes. Two to four players. Age ten and up. The rules are accessible. The strategy runs deep.
The Game
Players are research assistants competing to produce the most valuable corn kernels by pairing DNA cards.

Each round, a hand of cards is drafted — you choose one, pass the rest. From those cards you create kernels. Purple. Colorless. And the rare, coveted Speckled kernel — produced only when an Activator token is in play, just as McClintock’s jumping genes produced unpredictable bursts of color in real maize.

Kernels are placed on a shared Corn Cob board. Purple slots. Colorless slots. Speckled kernels go anywhere — wild cards that can connect groups, complete rows, and flip the score in a single placement.

Scoring is immediate but strategic. Connected kernels of the same color score bonus points. Completing a row earns a bonus token worth three to five points — revealed only at game end. Dormancy tokens let you hold kernels in reserve, timing their placement for maximum impact.
The game ends when any kernel type runs out. Unused Dormancy tokens score. Row Bonus tokens are revealed. The leaderboard can flip in the final count.
The Science
Every mechanic maps directly to real biology.

The DNA cards represent alleles. Pairing them mimics genetic crosses. Broken DNA cards require Repair tokens — reflecting real chromosomal damage and repair. The Activator token mirrors the Ac element McClintock discovered — the mobile genetic element that wakes up the jumping gene and produces that stunning speckle of color on a colorless kernel.

The score track spans McClintock’s entire life — from her birth in Hartford in 1902 to her centenary in 2002\. Each decade marks a moment in her story. A factoid. A bonus. A reminder of what she was up against — and what she achieved.
Barbara McClintock spent decades working alone, certain the world would eventually catch up with her.
It did.

McClintock’s Maize
Goal
Be the player with the most victory points at the end of the game.
Components
•  60 genetic tiles (15 each of Purple-Smooth, Purple-Wrinkled, Yellow-Smooth, Yellow-Wrinkled)
•  50 kernel cubes: • 18 Purple Smooth (1 pt) • 12 Purple Wrinkled (2 pts) • 9 Yellow Smooth (3 pts) • 6 Yellow Wrinkled (4 pts) • 5 Speckled (6 pts)
•  1 Corn Cob scoring board
•  1 First Player corn cob meeple
•  4 Microscope player tokens (one per player)
•  Normal Cell Boards (2 per player for 3–4 players, 3 per player for 2 players)
•  DS Cell Boards (1 per player)
•  10 Ac tokens
•  1 tile bag
Setup
1\.  Place the Corn Cob board in the center of the table.
2\.  In turn order, each player chooses one row on the Corn Cob board using their Microscope token. This is the only row where you may place your kernels.
3\.  Each player takes their starting Cell Boards: 2 normal boards (3 if playing with 2 players).
4\.  Shuffle all 60 tiles and place them in the bag.
Gameplay
The game lasts 5 rounds.
Each Round:
1\.  All players simultaneously draw 4 tiles from the bag.
2\.  Each player splits their 4 tiles into two piles of 2 and presents both piles to the player on their right.
3\.  The neighbor chooses one pile for themselves. The other pile returns to you.
4\.  Place one tile from each of the two piles onto each of your Cell Boards (one tile from your returned pile and one from your neighbor’s chosen pile on each board).
5\.  Each Cell Board produces one kernel cube based on the two tiles:
•  Color: Purple is dominant. Any purple \= purple. Two yellows \= yellow.
•  Texture: Smooth is dominant. Any smooth \= smooth. Two wrinkled \= wrinkled.
6\.  Place the produced cube on your chosen row on the Corn Cob board and score its point value.
7\.  Return all used tiles to the bag.
Transposon (DS) Cell Board:
Starting in round two, each player receives one DS Cell Board in addition to their normal boards. The DS board has a silencing spot in the upper left corner.
•  Any color gene placed in the silencing spot is silenced.
•  A silenced purple loses its dominance, allowing yellow to show.
•  If you place an Ac token on the DS board and a yellow allele is also present, you produce a Speckled kernel (6 pts) instead.
Running Out of Cubes:
If there are no more cubes of the type your cell board produces, you produce nothing that round. The tiles are still returned to the bag.
End of Round:
The first player token passes clockwise to the next player.
Game End:
After 5 rounds, the player with the most points wins.
